cells.tense: You're keeping the practice lit, and the solitude in it is where you refill rather than hide.
cells.ask: After one session this week, tell the person who'd ask about it what you actually did — one line, no more detail than they need.
cells.core:
You're keeping the practice lit. Not with flash — with a small steady light, tended on the days you'd rather not and tended anyway. That's what's carrying the load right now, and it's holding form without going hard about it.

The solitude works in your favor. You go quiet to refill, not to get away from people, and when you come back there's more of you to be around. When you finish a session, you let it be finished. That's the balance — refining serves the growing, not the worrying. The one place it could tip: you keep the practice so private that no one else ever gets to see its shape. You can spend a whole season on something real that's entirely yours, and nobody knows it exists. A practice can stay honest and still be invisible.
cells.sheetLine: The practice is steady, and the quiet works in your favor.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice lit by attention
cells.place: where you hold form under weight without going hard or going rigid

cells.tense: Ahead of you there's a version where the practice is finally beyond criticism, and you're already living there, refining toward it.
cells.ask: Before the next session, write down what would make it good enough — then do the session and stop at that line, even if the line is low.
cells.core:
Ahead of you sits the version where the practice is finally beyond criticism, and you're already living there. So every session becomes proof — and none of them quite pass. You finish one and the flaws are visible. The refining starts before the session ends. That's the shape too much takes here, and the cost is the thing refining was for.

It doesn't land, that measuring. No session ends with you done, because the next one is already being weighed against a standard that moved while you were working. Endurance turns into hardness — the grip is doing the work now, not the strength. Somewhere you suspect that stopping would prove something. It wouldn't. What you've done has already landed; it just hasn't been given permission to count.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing finishes, because you're already judging the next one.

cells.tense: Past experiences have made practice feel like a door you stopped knocking on, and you've been standing at its far side since.
cells.ask: Do one small version of the practice where someone can see you doing it — or share one session's result with one person, nothing more.
cells.core:
There's a door you're not knocking on. Solitude stopped being the place you refill and started being a place to stay out of reach, and you've been calling it not having time, or not being in the right season for it, while the seasons keep going.

What's still working is standing under weight. You bear up everywhere else, well enough that people don't notice the one spot where you won't pick anything back up. Nothing is broken; nothing is getting added back either, so the practice asks more of you than it used to and returns less. Pushing harder at the dry spot won't help. What refills it is a step out where the give and take are even — small, and seen by one other person, once.
cells.sheetLine: The practice isn't gone, it's just not getting picked back up.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice lit by attention
cells.place: where you hold form under weight without going hard or going rigid

cells.tense: You're keeping a practice right now and calling it something else — the pen is down, but the writing hasn't stopped.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you already do on a schedule and write down what it's built — two lines, plain, no explaining yourself.
cells.core:
You have something you do regularly — early, or late, or when the household doesn't need anything — and you'd not call it practice. You'd call it just how you get through, or just how you've managed it as long as you can remember. It's been building skill the whole time. That skill arrived without you noticing how, which is why it looks like something you just have.

What isn't claimed is that you're the one doing it. You move through a room, take its weight without thinking, and the fact that you lit that practice again today doesn't get your name on it anywhere. That's the gap — the doing is real, the saying-so isn't. Sitting with the ambiguity for an hour wouldn't fix it. A small, plain record of what's already yours would.
cells.sheetLine: The skill is real. What's missing is you calling it yours.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice lit by attention
cells.place: where you hold form under weight without going hard or going rigid

attempts.check: The record doesn't license a history, so Too Little must locate the person at a stopped practice without saying what made practice feel dangerous — no event, no person, no duration. The most likely objection is 'that's not what's happening — I just haven't started'; the ask survives being wrong because inviting one more person in is still a smaller, fairer calibration of a practice whether or not my read is right. The sentence that serves me more than them would be 'you're so disciplined' — praise for a method I invented, cut.
